body.text: P4M seeks to make flexible coalitions a means of strengthening multilateralism, but its credibility will depend on its ability to translate shared commitments into inclusive cooperation without deepening institutional fragmentation

The launch of Partners for Multilateralism, International Law, Peace and Prosperity (P4M) brings into focus a larger question: whether flexible coalitions can strengthen multilateralism or risk deepening its fragmentation. At a time when geopolitical rivalry, institutional gridlock and competing national interests are placing increasing pressure on universal institutions, P4M seeks to unite countries committed to the United Nations-centred order. Rather than replace existing multilateral structures, it aims to sustain cooperation and advance their reform in a changing international environment.

Launched during the 81st UN General Assembly High-Level Week in September 2026, P4M was initially co-sponsored by Australia, Barbados, Brazil, Canada, the European Union, India and Kenya. It subsequently attracted signatories including Albania, Armenia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Council of Europe, Croatia, Cyprus, Finland, Guatemala, Ireland, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, Moldova, Norway, San Marino, Slovakia, Spain, Türkiye and Uruguay. The signatory list extends the initiative’s geographical and institutional reach, although its early membership remains weighted towards European states. This weighting makes P4M’s commitment to inclusiveness a test it must meet in practice, rather than a feature it can claim.

P4M’s emergence reflects the diversification of international cooperation in recent decades. Traditional multilateral institutions increasingly coexist with more flexible forums, alliances and partnerships, including the G7, G20, BRICS, the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (Quad), and AUKUS (Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States). While these groupings differ in membership, objectives and institutional structures, they demonstrate how states pursue cooperation through overlapping platforms alongside universal institutions.

The political rationale articulated by P4M’s proponents also illustrates this shift. In a joint op-ed, European Council President António Costa, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Kenyan President William Ruto and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney described P4M as a “flexible, open framework” through which countries from different regions and political traditions could build coalitions across differences and translate shared principles into practical action. The four leaders present flexible cooperation not as an alternative to multilateralism but as a means of sustaining it and advancing institutional reform.

P4M stands apart for its explicit commitment to strengthening, rather than bypassing, the UN. Its declaration recognises the UN Charter-based system as indispensable while calling for its renewal and reform.

P4M stands apart for its explicit commitment to strengthening, rather than bypassing, the UN. Its declaration recognises the UN Charter-based system as indispensable while calling for its renewal and reform. The declaration proposes a more open, equitable, inclusive, networked and practical approach to cooperation, including closer partnerships with regional organisations and support for regional integration.

P4M’s declaration sets out an expansive agenda that goes beyond institutional reform to cover economic governance and emerging global challenges. It calls for more resilient and diversified supply chains, reform of the multilateral trading system, improvements to the international financial architecture and stronger coordination on digital transformation, artificial intelligence, climate change and global health. At the inaugural P4M summit, India’s External Affairs Minister added specificity to this economic agenda by highlighting the interconnected vulnerabilities of the ‘4F’ crisis of fuel, food, fertiliser and finance, and arguing for international frameworks and guardrails to address supply disruptions and the risks of chokepoint dominance.

The declaration also highlights rising inequalities within and among countries, identifying initiatives such as the Global Alliance Against Hunger and Poverty and the International Panel on Inequality as examples of collective efforts to address these challenges. It reaffirms the importance of implementing existing global frameworks, particularly the Paris Agreement and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.

P4M’s contribution to UN80 should be political rather than procedural: sustaining reform momentum, building member-state support and ensuring efficiency measures do not weaken development mandates or the voice of less powerful member states.

On institutional reform, the declaration specifically commits participants to supporting the United Nations through initiatives such as UN80. Launched by the UN Secretary-General in 2025, UN80 seeks to improve the organisation's efficiency and coherence through reforms to Secretariat operations, mandate implementation and review, and system-wide structures and programmes. As a member-state-led process, its outcomes remain subject to intergovernmental deliberation. P4M’s contribution to UN80 should be political rather than procedural: sustaining reform momentum, building member-state support and ensuring efficiency measures do not weaken development mandates or the voice of less powerful member states.

The declaration also commits signatories to regular exchanges with partners from all regions to foster dialogue, coordination and practical cooperation. While this provides an important starting point, the breadth of the initiative's agenda makes prioritisation essential. Its credibility will depend on whether these exchanges can identify areas of common interest, facilitate coordination and translate shared commitments into tangible outcomes.

Flexible cooperation can generate momentum where universal consensus is difficult to achieve. Selective participation, however, also raises questions about representation and accountability. Countries outside these arrangements may have limited opportunities to shape the priorities these arrangements advance, while the proliferation of initiatives risks duplicating existing efforts and creating competing agendas. The legitimacy of reform efforts also depends on whether their objectives and expected benefits are communicated beyond diplomatic circles, particularly to the populations affected by decisions taken through multilateral institutions.

These concerns are particularly relevant to P4M’s ambition of strengthening an inclusive multilateral order. Its commitment to openness and participation from all regions must be reflected in how the initiative develops: whose priorities inform its agenda, and how countries beyond its initial membership can contribute. Equally, regular exchanges must lead to more than recurring diplomatic consultations if P4M is to demonstrate practical value.

P4M offers an opportunity to demonstrate that flexibility and universality can reinforce one another. Its success will hinge on its ability to translate political alignment into practical cooperation without deepening the fragmentation it seeks to address.

Ultimately, P4M’s significance will depend on whether it can make flexible cooperation complement universal institutions. A more diverse network of partnerships and platforms may help sustain multilateral action, but it cannot substitute for the legitimacy and participation of the wider international community. P4M offers an opportunity to demonstrate that flexibility and universality can reinforce one another. Its success will hinge on its ability to translate political alignment into practical cooperation without deepening the fragmentation it seeks to address.
